results.summary: The Retro Console is an 8.5-bit game console implemented in Verilog that generates VGA video and audio. It includes a PPU that produces pixels from tile, map, and sprite data, and a synthesizer that mixes four voices at 96 kHz. The design is tested using an RP2040-based RAM emulator that provides program and graphics data, with VGA output via a Pmod and audio output left to external hardware. Silicon tests confirm the graphics work, but the synth portion has not been tested.

VGA Experiments in Tennis is a simple Pong-like game implemented in Verilog. It uses VGA output to display paddles and a ball, with inputs for paddle movement, score reset, and speed selection. The design requires a VGA Pmod and buttons for gameplay. Silicon tests confirm it works with both Mole99 and Digilent VGA Pmods.

Silly 4b CPU v2 is a minimal 4-bit CPU inspired by the PDP-8, implemented in Verilog. It features 8 words of 6-bit memory, a 4-bit accumulator, and a 3-bit program counter, and can execute simple programs like Fibonacci. The CPU is controlled via input pins for commands and arguments, and outputs the accumulator and program counter. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected.

NCL LFSR is a self-timed logic experiment implementing a linear-feedback shift register using null convention logic. The design uses dual-rail encoding to distinguish data from null, and includes an oscillator for random number generation. Testing requires an oscilloscope to observe the signals. Silicon tests show the C-gate works, but the oscillator does not function as expected.

Convertidor de Tiempo a Digital (TDC) is a time-to-digital converter that measures the width of an input pulse and transmits the digital value via RS232. It includes a counter, a state machine, and an RS232 transmitter operating at 9600 baud with odd parity. The design is intended for interfacing with time-output sensors and was tested in simulation and on an FPGA development board.

Triple Watchdog is a redundant watchdog timer implemented in Verilog, consisting of three watchdog modules operating in lockstep. Each watchdog must be kicked by writing a different value to the input within a 1 ms timeout; otherwise, it sets an output pin high. The design is intended as part of a larger fault-tolerant supervisor system. No silicon test reports are provided.

Dickson Charge Pump is an analog circuit that boosts the input voltage to approximately 5.4 V using a 3-stage Dickson charge pump. The output voltage is divided by 6 for measurement due to the 1.8 V analog pin limit. It requires a 2 MHz clock input and was tested at various frequencies, showing best performance at 5-10 MHz. Silicon tests confirm it works, with output voltage around 4.3 V at optimal frequencies.

DFFRAM Example (128 bytes) is a 128-byte RAM module implemented using a 32x32 1RW DFFRAM macro. It provides an 8-bit address bus, 8-bit data input, and 8-bit data output, with a write-enable pin. The RAM contents are not reset by the system reset. The design is a simple memory block for integration into larger systems.

Simon Says game is a memory game implemented in Verilog where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors. It uses four LEDs, four buttons, a speaker for tones, and a two-digit 7-segment display for the score. The design requires external hardware including buttons, LEDs, and optionally a speaker and 7-segment display. Silicon tests confirm it works with a Simon Says PMOD.

SPELL is a hardware implementation of a minimal, stack-based programming language created for The Skull CTF. It features 32 bytes of program memory, 32 bytes of stack, and 8 I/O pins, with a serial interface for loading programs and inspecting state. The design is tested by loading and executing SPELL programs, and silicon tests confirm it can run a program that spells 'SPELL' on a 7-segment display.
